plain: The story is that a British Museum scholar named George Smith spent about ten years on a mass of clay tablets from ancient Nineveh and found among them the Gilgamesh epic and its flood story. Matt LaCroix, a researcher of ancient history, tells it in brief: Smith "gets a hold of these, he brings it back to the British Museum," and spends "10 years studying them." The fuller account comes from the introduction to The Babylonian Story of the Deluge and the Epic of Gilgamish, published by the British Museum in 1920 with translations by the scholar E. A. Wallis Budge. Budge writes that the tablets "discovered by Layard and Rassam at Nineveh came to the British Museum in 1854-5," that the Trustees "employed George Smith" in 1866 to sort and rejoin the fragments, and that he found "the adventures of Gilgamish, an ancient king of Erech" and "an account of the Deluge," which he published in December 1872. He adds that in digs at Kuyûnjik, a mound at Nineveh, in 1873 and 1874 Smith "recovered many fragments" that let him complete the twelve tablets, and that he "died of hunger and sickness near Aleppo in 1876." Read this way, the first tablets reached the museum through other men, so LaCroix's picture of Smith bringing them back fits the later fragments rather than the collection Smith first read. His years on the tablets, 1866 to 1876, come close to LaCroix's ten. The story matters because it is how the world first learned of a flood story older than the Bible's.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: In the introduction to The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, Budge writes that the tablets "discovered by Layard and Rassam at Nineveh came to the British Museum in 1854-5", that the Trustees "employed George Smith" in 1866 to sort and rejoin them, that he found among them the Gilgamish tablets and the Deluge account, published in December 1872, and that "During the excavations which Smith carried out at Kuyûnjik in 1873 and 1874 he recovered many fragments" before he died in 1876. In this account the first tablets reached the museum through Layard and Rassam, and Smith's own finds at Nineveh are the further fragments of 1873 and 1874; the teller's picture of Smith bringing the tablets to the museum fits those later fragments, not the collection he first read. His years on the tablets run from 1866 to 1876, close to the teller's ten.
